Buckland
BUK-land
n. (a Cistercian abbey in Devon, founded 1278 by Amicia countess of Devon; after the dissolution it became the house of Sir Francis Drake)
Old English bocland, book-land — land held by written charter rather than by folk custom.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Buckland was founded in 1278 by Amicia, countess of Devon, one of the last Cistercian houses established in England. It was surrendered in 1541, sold to Sir Richard Grenville, and in 1581 bought by Sir Francis Drake, who turned the abbey church itself into a dwelling — the nave floored across, a hall and chambers inside the walls, the tower a stair. The house still stands and is still called Buckland Abbey, and a man may walk through a Cistercian church that has been a sea captain's parlour for four hundred years. Jeremiah's lament over a conquered Jerusalem is the text, and it is not comfortable for either side of the Reformation argument: “Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2). Moses had warned Israel about the opposite danger, of receiving “houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not” (Deu 6:11) and forgetting who gave them. Buckland is both warnings in one building: a house lost by those who misused it, and gained by men who did not build it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; and alien as a foreigner, one born in or belonging to another country.

expand to see more

INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession or in course of law; an estate which a man has by descent.

ALIEN, n. A foreigner; one born in or belonging to another country; one who is not a denizen or entitled to the privileges of a citizen.

CHARTER, n. A written instrument, executed with usual forms, given as evidence of a grant, contract, or whatever is done between man and man.

STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country. One of another town, city, state or province in the same nation.

DWELLING, n. Habitation; place of residence; abode.

Key Scripture

Lam 5:2 — "Our inheritance is turned to strangers, our houses to aliens."

Deu 6:11 — "And houses full of all good things, which thou filledst not, and wells digged, which thou diggedst not, vineyards and olive trees, which thou plantedst not; when thou shalt have eaten and be full;"

Deu 6:12 — "Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage."

Psa 24:1 — "A Psalm of David. The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein."

Modern Corruption

A Cistercian church with a sea captain's hall built inside it, and the two warnings that meet in one building.

expand to see more

The corruption is the transfer of church property into private hands as the real engine of the English dissolution — a reform whose doctrine was often sound and whose beneficiaries were courtiers. It will not do for a Protestant dictionary to pretend otherwise. Moses foresaw the spiritual danger of such a windfall precisely: “Then beware lest thou forget the LORD, which brought thee forth out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage” (Deu 6:12).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no title to land is absolute, because “The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein” (Psa 24:1). Monks held Buckland on that condition and lost it; Drake held it on the same condition and so do its present trustees. Book-land is still only book-land.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English bocland, land held by charter; Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Hebrew zur (H2114), a stranger; Hebrew nokri (H5237), a foreigner; Hebrew melo (H4393), fulness.

expand to see more

Old English boc + land — land conveyed by a written book or charter.

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession; “Our inheritance is turned to strangers” (Lam 5:2).

Hebrew nokri (H5237) — a foreigner, an alien; “our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2).

Hebrew chaphar (H2658) — to dig; “and wells digged, which thou diggedst not” (Deu 6:11).

Hebrew melo (H4393) — fulness, that which fills; “and the fulness thereof” (Psa 24:1).

Usage

"“our houses to aliens” (Lam 5:2) — said in 1541 and meant literally."

"“beware lest thou forget the LORD” (Deu 6:12) — the warning to the man who inherits."

"“The earth is the LORD'S” (Psa 24:1) — the only deed that is final."
